newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE-Lone woman fasts in jail full of Mexican men.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Lone woman fasts in jail full of Mexican men.

text.p: The jail is known as the second toughest in all of Mexico, one of the country's two maximum security prisons and a place where hardened drug dealers and killers are sent.

So human rights groups want to know why Ana Maria Vera Smith is there. The 40-year-old radical leftist was imprisoned on kidnapping charges in 1990 and has been held for seven years without a trial because of witnesses who failed to show up and allegations that she was tortured into confessing.

Calling herself a political prisoner, Vera Smith has staged hunger strikes to end her status as the only woman in Puente Grande prison in the western state of Jalisco, which holds about 900 men. She has a tiny cell to herself in the prison, where she was whisked last September for reasons her backers say are still not clear.

Surrounded by some of Mexico's most dangerous criminals, she gets just two hours of exercise a day and is searched repeatedly and degradingly by the prison's male guards, human rights advocates say. Pablo Garcia, coordinator of the National Committee for the Defence of Political Prisoners, told Reuters Vera Smith is being punished for a crime for which she was never convicted or sentenced.
"She is the only woman in a men's jail. By law only men and already sentenced convicts are allowed there," he said.
Puente Grande is Mexico's second toughest prison after the feared Almoloya, just outside Mexico City. It houses drug traffickers, murderers and gangsters.
GOVERNMENT HAS NO COMMENT

Prison authorities declined comment about the status of Vera Smith, but a source at the government's National Human Rights Commission, who asked not to be identified, confirmed it was aware of her situation.

"In October we received a complaint regarding the violation of individual guarantees of Ana Maria Vera Smith. We are investigating and we will determine whether to make a recommendation or not," the source said.

Meanwhile, since March 10, Vera Smith has held a series of 72-hour hunger strikes to press for her removal from Puente Grande, where she is held in a cell just big enough for a bed, a stone chair, a shower and a toilet, Garcia said.

"She only has access two hours a day to a space of five yards (metres) by 10 yards (metres) to walk in. She is forced to work, sewing pillow cases and sheets, and she is obliged to do junior high school courses even though she has a degree in psychology," he said.
The mother of two is a well-known radical whose supporters say she is jailed for her beliefs and is innocent of the kidnapping charges against her.
ACCUSED WITH HUSBAND OF KIDNAPPING

Vera Smith and her husband, Felipe Edgardo Canceso Ruiz, are accused of kidnapping Kazusigue Sekiguchi, a Mexican of Japanese ancestry who human rights groups say never saw the people accused of seizing him. The couple was moved to Puente Grande from a jail in Mexico City in September just after a rebel group calling itself the Popular Revolutionary Army emerged in southern Mexico.

They were not charged with belonging to a rebel group but before their arrests seven years ago they had had long links to radical politics in southern Mexico. Also accused in the kidnapping was David Cabanas Barrientos, brother of Lucio Cabanas who led a guerrilla movement in the southern state of Guerrero in the 1970s before he was killed by the army.

Human rights officials have long contended the confessions the suspects supposedly signed were forced out of them through torture. In 1992, their case was mentioned in a report on Mexico by the United Nations Human Rights Commission.

"During seven days, and under permament threat of death, they were harshly beaten, they suffered attempts to asphyxiate them by putting a plastic bag over their heads and with their heads submerged underwater they were given electric shocks and were burned with cigarettes," the report said.

According to Garcia, the psychological torture continues. He said Vera Smith is allowed to see her husband for two hours every nine days, without physical contact, and has not seen her children, who are now 9 and 11, for 13 months.
In jail the scrutiny is rigorous. The all-male guards inspect her up to 14 times a day, Garcia said, "in a degrading manner designed to intimidate her."

Aurelia Perez Cano, a lawyer who defends women's rights, said Vera Smith's detention was unconstitutional because the law states that women can be jailed only with other women, and maximum-security prisons are meant only for male convicts.
The government says women can be sent there as well.
